migrationNotes: Spine: a tiny shop program that starts as one line, then grows: a name stores an answer and forgets the rule, a name can update itself, and a notebook kernel keeps all of it between runs.
The spreadsheet in the opener is the contrast the whole lesson comes back to: a sheet keeps rules, Python keeps answers.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): python-run-and-bind-hook (the spreadsheet sum, covered by the opener).

lesson.title: Follow a value through a program

lead.text: A Python program is a list of instructions, written one to a line. Python reads them from the top and carries out each one in turn, so the order you write them in is the order things happen. The most common instruction gives a value a name.

Say a shop sells pens at 4 each. The line price = 4 stores the number 4 under the name price. A labelled jar is a good picture: the name is the label and the value is what's inside. The equals sign here is an instruction to store, and it says nothing about whether two things match. An instruction of this kind is called an assignment.

The right-hand side can be a calculation. For total = price * 3, Python reads price and finds 4, then multiplies it by 3 and puts the answer, 12, in a new jar labelled total. The star is Python's multiplication sign. You can also leave a note for people reading the program: a line that starts with # is a comment, and Python skips it.
Python has reached the line price = 4, and nothing else has run yet. Think about what the line leaves behind once it has finished.

Return to the spreadsheet, where changing A1 rewrote B1 for you. A short program shows how Python differs. Step through the lines in the picture and watch the two names, price and total. The small int label beside each value only says it is a whole number, which the next lesson explains.

afterFigure.text: After line 3, price holds 6 and total still holds 12. When Python ran line 2 it read price, which was 4 at that moment, worked out 4 × 3 and stored the answer. The name total keeps only that answer. It has no record of the calculation behind it, so changing price later cannot reach back and alter it.

The second case in the picture shows the only way to get a total of 18. You run the calculation again, by writing total = price * 3 a second time after price has changed. Python works out each line when it reaches it, and the result stays in its name until a later line stores something else there.

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
price = 4
total = price * 3
price = 6
total = price * 3

lead.text: Here is the same pattern with new numbers. The program stores price and uses it to work out total. Then it changes price. Decide what total holds at the end.

steps.headline: Changing a name using its own value

lead.text: A line can change a name by building on what it already holds. Take x = 3 followed by x = x + 2. Python always works out the right-hand side first, using the value x holds at that moment, which is 3. It gets 5 and stores that under x, which replaces the old 3.

Storing a new value under a name that already has one is called reassignment. Adding to a name is so common that Python has a shorthand: the line x += 2 means exactly the same as x = x + 2. A running total in a data program is usually built this way, with each line reading the name and putting back an adjusted value.
To say what a name holds at any point, read the lines above that point and apply them in order. Skip the comments, since Python does. Whatever the last line stored under the name is what it holds.
Comments change nothing, so they are easy to trace. Work through the program line by line and ignore anything Python would skip.

So far the lines ran from top to bottom in one go. Most data analysis happens in a notebook instead, a page made of separate boxes called cells, each holding a few lines of Python. You run a cell by pressing a button, and you may run any cell, in any order, as many times as you like.

Something has to remember the names between those runs. It is a program called the kernel, which sits behind the notebook and keeps a record of every name and its value. Run a cell that sets count = 2 and the kernel holds count at 2. Run a different cell later and it finds count still there.
Put together, a notebook is one long program that you feed in pieces. The kernel keeps its names until you restart it, and then they are all gone.

steps.headline: A notebook cell sets count = 2. Then a second cell, count += 3, is run twice. What is count?

lead.text: The kernel's memory does the work here. Follow count through each run.

workedSteps.text: The first cell stores 2 under count.
Run the second cell once. count += 3 means count = count + 3.
Run it again. It starts from the value the kernel kept.

steps.headline: A notebook starts with count = 1. You run count += 4 three times. What is count at the end?

workedSteps.text: Start with count = 1. The first run adds 4.
The second run adds 4 to the kept value. What is count now?
The third run adds 4 again. What is count at the end?

steps.headline: Why the order of runs matters

lead.text: Because the kernel remembers, the order in which you run cells decides what it holds, and that order need not match the order down the page. Say cell 1 sets days = 3 and cell 2 works out hours = days * 24, so hours is 72.

Now go back and edit cell 1 to days = 5, and run only that cell. The kernel holds days at 5, but hours is still 72, because the line that works it out has not run again. Run cell 2 and hours becomes 120. Until you do, the page shows code that no longer matches what the kernel holds.

This is why a notebook can mislead. The page can look right while the kernel holds results from older runs. The check is to restart the kernel and run every cell from the top, in page order. If the results still make sense, nothing in the notebook depends on an old run.
Three cells share one kernel. Think about which value of rate the kernel holds when cell 2 runs for the second time.

lesson.orientation: Track assignment and execution order, then make a notebook reproducible.

lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Open a spreadsheet and type 5 into A1. In B1 type =A1*4, and B1 shows 20. Now change A1 to 9. B1 changes to 36 without you touching it, because B1 holds a rule and the sheet applies that rule again whenever A1 changes.

Python is a language for giving a computer written instructions, and much of modern data analysis is done in it. It behaves differently from a spreadsheet. When Python works something out it keeps the answer and forgets how it got there. That difference explains most of the surprises a newcomer meets, and it decides which numbers you can trust when you return to a piece of work an hour later.

This lesson follows one number through a tiny shop program. It starts with a single line, to see what Python keeps. After that it moves to the kind of page where analysts usually work, and there the order you run lines in starts to matter.

intro.promise: By the end you'll follow a value through a Python program line by line, and say what a notebook still remembers.

recap.keyIdea: A name holds the value it was given at that line. Python runs lines in order, and a notebook kernel keeps every name between runs.

blocks.text: Back at the spreadsheet, B1 follows a rule and a Python name keeps an answer. You saw total hold 20 after price changed, counted a notebook up to 13 across three runs, and worked out that running cell 2 again reads the newest rate.

recap.nextHook: Every value so far was a number, yet a name can also hold text, and Python treats the text '12' very differently from the number 12. The next lesson sorts out which is which and shares eleven biscuits between four plates.

questions.prompt: Set price = 5, then total = price * 4, then price = 9. What value does total keep?
hints: Which value did price hold when total was stored?
total was stored before price changed.
Work out 5 × 4 once; the later assignment affects only price.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: total was assigned 5 × 4 = 20. Reassigning price does not run the earlier multiplication again.

questions.onCorrect: 20. total stored the result of 5 × 4 at its own line; changing price afterwards left it alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That recalculates with the new price, as a spreadsheet would. Python stored total before the price changed.
That is the final price. The question asks what total keeps.

questions.prompt: A notebook starts with count = 1, and you run count += 4 three times. What is count after the third run?
hints: Start from the value after the second run.
Add 4 once more.
Work out 9 + 4.
questions.onCorrect: 13. Three runs add 4 three times to the starting 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts three lots of 4 but forgets the starting 1.
That is the value after the second run. The third run adds 4 more.

questions.prompt: The program sets x = 3, then has the line # x = 50, then y = x * 2. What is y?
hints: Which of these lines does Python actually run?
A line starting with # is only a note.
Work out 3 × 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The comment is skipped, so x is 3 and y is 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The comment never ran, so x stayed 3. Only statements change what a name holds.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses x = 50. The line starting with # is a comment, so it never ran.
The comment did not run, so x is not 50.

questions.prompt: A notebook's first cell sets rate = 2, and its second cell sets total = rate * 10. A third cell sets rate = 5. You run the cells in that order and then run only the second cell again. What is total now?
hints: Which value of rate does the kernel hold when cell 2 runs again?
Cell 3 changed rate before cell 2 ran the second time.
Work out 5 × 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The kernel holds rate = 5, so cell 2 gives 5 × 10 = 50.

questions.onCorrect: 50. Cell 2 read the newest rate the kernel held, so the result depends on the run order.

misconceptions.feedback: That is total from the first run. Cell 2 ran again, now with the newer rate.
That is only the multiplier. Multiply it by the rate the kernel holds.

questions.prompt: Set units = 6 and cost = 7, then calculate total = units * cost. What is total?
hints: Substitute both stored values.
The calculation multiplies the two names.
Work out 6 × 7.
questions.onCorrect: 42. The line reads the stored values of units and cost and multiplies them.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the values. The line uses *, which multiplies.

questions.prompt: A script sets x = 3, then x = x + 2, then y = x * 4. What is y?
hints: Follow the lines in order.
x changes before y is worked out.
Work out (3 + 2) × 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second line makes x equal 5; the last line gives 5 × 4 = 20.

questions.onCorrect: 20. x = x + 2 stores 5 under x, and y then uses that new value.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the old x = 3. The second line changed x before y was calculated.
That is 3 + 2 + 4. The last line multiplies.

hints: Did cell 2 run again after the edit?
m was stored from the first run of cell 2.
Work out 3 + 4.
questions.prompt: Cell 1 sets k = 3 and cell 2 sets m = k + 4. You change cell 1 to k = 10 and run only cell 1. What is m now?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: m keeps 3 + 4 = 7 until cell 2 is run again.

questions.onCorrect: 7. m was stored when cell 2 last ran. Editing and running cell 1 does not recalculate it.

misconceptions.feedback: That recalculates with the new k. Cell 2 has not run again, so m still holds the older result.
That is the new k. The question asks for m.

hints: B1's formula refers to A1. What is in A1 now?
The formula multiplies A1 by 4.
Work out 9 × 4.
questions.prompt: What number does B1 show now?
questions.onCorrect: 36. A spreadsheet formula recalculates when its inputs change. Python assignments behave differently, as the next screens show.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B1 before the change. A spreadsheet formula recalculates when A1 changes.
That adds 4 instead of multiplying. The formula is =A1*4.

hints: Think about what happens when the line runs, not what it promises later.
questions.prompt: What does the line price = 4 do?

choices.label: Promises that price will always equal 4

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An assignment stores the value in the name once, when the line runs.

questions.onCorrect: It stores the value 4 under the name price. A later line can store a different value under the same name.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how a spreadsheet rule behaves. An assignment runs once; nothing keeps it true afterwards.
A question about equality uses a double equals sign. One equals sign stores a value.

hints: Where does the second run get its starting value from?
questions.prompt: Why does the second run give 8 rather than 5?

choices.label: The kernel kept count = 5 from the first run.
Each run starts again from the first cell.

acceptedIdeas: The kernel kept count = 5 from the first run.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The kernel keeps names between cell runs, so each run starts from the last value.

questions.onCorrect: The kernel kept count = 5, so the second run adds 3 to that.

misconceptions.feedback: Then every run would give 5. The kernel does not rewind between runs.
The statement adds 3 to whatever count holds. The result depends on the starting value.

hints: Start from the value the kernel kept, 5.
Add 4 to it.
Work out 5 + 4.
questions.prompt: What is count after the second run?
questions.onCorrect: 9. Each run adds 4 to whatever the kernel kept.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value after the first run. The second run adds 4 more.
That is only the amount added. Add it to the kept value.
